cloze.text: The current periodontal classification (AAP/EFP World Workshop 2017, published 2018) groups periodontal health with {{c1::gingivitis: dental biofilm-induced}} and {{c2::gingival diseases: non-dental biofilm-induced}}.
In the 2017 AAP classification the three forms of periodontitis are {{c1::necrotizing periodontal diseases}}, periodontitis, and {{c2::periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease}}.

'Other conditions affecting the periodontium' (2017 AAP) include systemic diseases affecting the supporting tissues, {{c1::periodontal abscesses and endodontic-periodontal lesions}}, {{c2::mucogingival deformities and conditions}}, {{c3::traumatic occlusal forces}}, and tooth- and prosthesis-related factors.
cloze.extra: AAP 2017: periodontal abscesses and endodontic-periodontal lesions sit under 'Other conditions affecting the periodontium' (with systemic diseases, mucogingival deformities, traumatic occlusal forces, tooth/prosthesis factors). The book prints them under the Periodontitis heading — the exam follows the AAP chart.

cloze.text: Peri-implant diseases and conditions (2017 AAP): peri-implant health, {{c1::peri-implant mucositis}}, {{c2::peri-implantitis}}, and {{c3::peri-implant soft and hard tissue deficiencies}}.

The AAP gingival-health categories are health on an {{c1::intact periodontium}}, health on a reduced periodontium in a {{c2::previously treated (stable) periodontitis}} patient, and health on a reduced periodontium in a {{c3::non-periodontitis}} patient.
Bleeding on probing at {{c1::less than 10%}} of sites is required for health in any diagnosis; BOP of {{c2::10% or greater}} means gingivitis.
Clinical health on an intact periodontium: BOP <10%, probing depths {{c1::1–3 mm}}, and {{c2::no CAL and no RBL}}.
Clinical gingival health on a reduced periodontium in a stable periodontitis patient: BOP <10%, probing depths {{c1::4 mm or less}}, CAL present, RBL present.
Clinical gingival health on a reduced periodontium in a non-periodontitis patient: BOP <10%, PD 1–3 mm, CAL present, RBL {{c1::possible}}.
cloze.extra: Stable perio patient: RBL present. Non-perio patient: RBL possible.

cloze.text: Plaque-induced gingivitis is prevalent at all ages and is considered the {{c1::most common form of periodontal disease}}.
The initial changes from health to plaque-induced gingivitis may {{c1::not be detectable clinically}}.
Common clinical signs of plaque-induced gingivitis: {{c1::erythema}}, {{c2::edema}}, bleeding, tenderness, and {{c3::enlargement}}.
Plaque-induced gingivitis begins at the {{c1::gingival margin}} and may spread throughout the remaining gingival unit.
Patients with gingivitis may notice bleeding with brushing, blood in saliva, gingival swelling and redness, and — in established forms — {{c1::halitosis}}.
The severity of plaque-induced gingivitis can be influenced by {{c1::tooth and root anatomy}}, restorative and endodontic considerations, and other tooth-related factors.
In plaque-induced gingivitis, radiographs and probing attachment levels generally show {{c1::no loss of supporting structures}}.
Plaque-induced gingivitis can also occur on a {{c1::reduced periodontium}}; it presents as gingival inflammation only, with {{c2::no progression of attachment loss}}.
In gingivitis, probing depths are 1–3 mm, but {{c1::pseudopocketing}} and {{c2::gingival overgrowth}} may make probe depths deeper.
cloze.extra: Gingivitis tables: intact periodontium — no CAL, no RBL; reduced, stable perio pt — CAL + RBL present; reduced, non-perio pt — CAL present, RBL possible. All BOP ≥10%.

cloze.text: Epithelial change in gingivitis: {{c1::elongation of the epithelial ridges (rete pegs)}} extending deeper into the gingival connective tissue.
Vascular change in gingivitis: {{c1::dilated capillaries}} next to the junctional epithelium increase blood flow, causing clinical redness and bleeding.
Connective-tissue breakdown in gingivitis: progressive destruction of the {{c1::collagen fiber network}}.
In the gingivitis cellular infiltrate, {{c1::neutrophils}} are often the first responders.
Lymphocytes in the gingivitis infiltrate — specifically {{c1::T-cells and B-cells}} — are key players in the immune response.
In gingivitis, {{c1::mast cells}} are involved in the initial inflammatory response.
{{c1::Fibroblasts}} — the resident cells that produce collagen and other connective-tissue components — show alterations as the tissue remodels under inflammation.
A {{c1::thick biofilm}} on the tooth surface initiates and sustains the inflammatory changes of gingivitis.
In gingivitis the gingival crevicular fluid contains high levels of {{c1::bacteria}} and {{c2::inflammatory mediators}}.

Sex steroid hormone fluctuations ({{c1::puberty, menstrual cycle, pregnancy, oral contraceptives}}) exaggerate the gingival response to plaque because of {{c2::increased vascularity}} and altered immune response.
cloze.extra: Category: systemic (hormonal & immunological) factor

cloze.text: Poorly controlled diabetes (especially Type 1) causes severe gingival inflammation because of {{c1::impaired immune response}} and altered wound healing.
cloze.extra: Category: systemic factor (hyperglycemia)

cloze.text: In {{c1::leukemia}}, thrombocytopenia and clotting-factor deficiencies cause pronounced gingival enlargement and bleeding that can mask or exacerbate gingivitis.
As a modifying factor, vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) causes severe gingival inflammation, bleeding, and impaired {{c1::collagen formation}}, exaggerating plaque-induced gingivitis.
cloze.extra: Category: systemic factor (malnutrition). See also scurvy as a direct cause of non-biofilm gingivitis.

cloze.text: The {{c1::level of plaque control}} is a direct, modifiable behavior that dictates the presence and severity of gingivitis; plaque is the primary cause, and its amount contributes to disease.
{{c1::Overhanging or poorly contoured subgingival restoration margins}} create plaque traps the patient cannot clean, causing localized plaque accumulation and persistent inflammation.
cloze.extra: Category: local (oral) factor

cloze.text: {{c1::Hyposalivation (dry mouth)}} reduces natural oral cleansing and makes mechanical plaque removal harder, increasing plaque and worsening gingival inflammation.
cloze.extra: Category: local (oral) factor

cloze.text: In non-dental biofilm-induced gingival disease the gingiva is inflamed {{c1::even without biofilm}} (a manifestation of a systemic condition), yet plaque accumulation {{c2::can still affect its clinical course}}.
{{c1::Hereditary gingival fibromatosis}} (a genetic/developmental abnormality) causes gingival overgrowth ranging from mild to severe, often {{c2::firm and pink}}.
Necrotizing gingivitis requires biofilm, but its primary driver is a {{c1::suppressed host immune response}} (e.g., stress, malnutrition, HIV/AIDS).
cloze.extra: AAP 2017 classifies necrotizing gingivitis under Necrotizing Periodontal Diseases (Periodontitis group); the book lists it in this table as a bacterial specific infection.

cloze.text: Necrotizing gingivitis presents with painful {{c1::punched-out papillae}}, a {{c2::pseudomembrane}}, and {{c3::fetid odor}}.
Herpetic gingivostomatitis: vesicles that quickly rupture into painful, fibrin-coated, irregular ulcers; usually seen in {{c1::young children}} as a {{c2::primary infection}}.
cloze.extra: Viral origin

cloze.text: {{c1::Coxsackie viruses}} (e.g., hand-foot-and-mouth disease) cause contagious vesicular lesions of the skin and oral mucosa, including the gingiva.
{{c1::Human papillomavirus (HPV)}} can manifest as papillomas or warts on the gingiva.
The most common gingival presentation of candidiasis (Candida albicans) is {{c1::redness of the attached gingiva}}, often with a granular surface.
cloze.extra: Fungal origin

cloze.text: Oral candidiasis can be white {{c1::pseudomembranous}} or {{c2::erythematous}}.

{{c1::Contact allergy}}: reaction to dental materials (e.g., flavoring agents in toothpaste, metals), foods, or other substances, with redness, swelling, burning, or discomfort localized to the contact area.

{{c1::Erythema multiforme}}: an acute, self-limiting immune-inflammatory disorder of mucosa and skin, with {{c2::target lesions}} on the skin and bullae/ulcers in the mouth, often with severe crusting of the lips.
{{c1::Pemphigus vulgaris}} is a chronic autoimmune disease with {{c2::intraepithelial}} bullae in skin and mucous membranes; oral lesions rupture quickly, leaving painful persistent erosions.
When pemphigus vulgaris affects the gingiva it appears as {{c1::desquamative gingivitis}}.
{{c1::Pyogenic granuloma}} (a reactive process) is a benign, rapidly growing, highly vascular lesion that bleeds easily, often on the gingiva.
Pyogenic granuloma is exacerbated by local irritation or hormonal changes (the "{{c1::pregnancy tumor}}"); despite its name it is {{c2::not pus-producing}}.
{{c1::Erythroplakia}} is a flat or slightly depressed red patch with a significantly {{c2::higher malignant potential}} than leukoplakia.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the gingiva can present as a persistent non-healing ulcer, a red or white lesion, or an {{c1::exophytic mass}}; it occurs most often in the {{c2::mandibular premolar and molar}} region.

Severe, prolonged vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) causes generalized gingival bleeding, swelling, soreness and impaired wound healing — it {{c1::directly causes}} gingival inflammation rather than merely exacerbating plaque-induced gingivitis.
cloze.extra: Category: endocrine, nutritional, metabolic

cloze.text: {{c1::Frictional keratosis}} is a white lesion caused by chronic mechanical irritation (e.g., rough restorations, cheek biting, vigorous brushing).
cloze.extra: Category: traumatic lesions

cloze.text: Toothbrushing-induced ulceration (aggressive or improper brushing/flossing) causes localized ulceration and inflammation, often at the {{c1::tips of the interdental papillae or the marginal gingiva}}.

{{c1::Smoker's melanosis}} is benign, irregular brown-to-black melanin pigmentation of the gingiva, most common on the {{c2::anterior facial gingiva}} — a physiological response to chemicals in tobacco smoke.
cloze.extra: Category: gingival pigmentation

cloze.text: Periodontitis is a chronic, multifactorial inflammatory disease associated with plaque biofilm that progressively destroys the tooth-supporting structures: CAL via {{c1::apical migration of the junctional epithelium}}, radiographic {{c2::alveolar bone loss}}, pocketing and gingival bleeding.

2017 periodontitis case definition: interdental CAL detectable at {{c1::two or more nonadjacent teeth}}, OR facial/lingual CAL of {{c2::3 mm or more}} with pocketing greater than 3 mm at two or more teeth.
To diagnose periodontitis, the CAL must not be due to {{c1::non-periodontitis causes}} such as trauma or orthodontics.
Once diagnosed, periodontitis is characterized by {{c1::staging}} (severity and complexity) and {{c2::grading}} (rate of progression).
The older terms "{{c1::chronic}}" and "{{c2::aggressive}}" periodontitis are now grouped simply under "periodontitis".
Staging depends on the {{c1::severity}} of disease at presentation and the {{c2::complexity}} of disease management, plus the extent and distribution in the dentition.
The initial stage is determined using {{c1::clinical attachment loss}}; if that is not available, {{c2::radiographic bone loss}} is used.
cloze.extra: Board Alert: memorize the staging and grading charts — they are not given on the exam.

cloze.text: Tooth loss due to periodontitis may modify the stage, and one or more complexity factors may shift the stage {{c1::to a higher level}}.
Staging by interdental CAL (site of greatest loss): Stage I {{c1::1–2 mm}}, Stage II {{c2::3–4 mm}}, Stages III and IV {{c3::≥5 mm}}.
Staging by radiographic bone loss: Stage I {{c1::coronal third (<15%)}}, Stage II {{c2::coronal third (15–33%)}}, Stages III and IV {{c3::extending to the middle third of the root and beyond}}.
Staging by tooth loss due to periodontitis: Stages I–II {{c1::no tooth loss}}, Stage III {{c2::≤4 teeth}}, Stage IV {{c3::≥5 teeth}}.
Local complexity: Stage I = maximum probing depth {{c1::≤4 mm}}; Stage II = maximum probing depth {{c2::≤5 mm}}; both with mostly {{c3::horizontal}} bone loss.
Stage III complexity (in addition to Stage II): probing depths {{c1::≥6 mm}}, vertical bone loss {{c2::≥3 mm}}, furcation involvement {{c3::Class II or III}}, moderate ridge defects.

Stage IV complexity: need for complex rehabilitation due to masticatory dysfunction, secondary occlusal trauma (tooth mobility {{c1::degree ≥2}}), severe ridge defects, bite collapse/drifting/flaring, and fewer than {{c2::20}} remaining teeth (10 opposing pairs).
Extent is added to the stage as a descriptor: localized (<30% of teeth), generalized, or {{c1::molar/incisor pattern}}.
{{c1::Stage I}} periodontitis represents the early stage of attachment loss — the borderland between gingivitis and periodontitis, a response to persistent gingival inflammation.
cloze.extra: Managed with standard treatment: personal and professional bacterial removal to arrest progression.

cloze.text: Stage III periodontitis: significant damage with deep lesions to the middle of the root, intrabony defects, furcation involvement and periodontal tooth loss; management is complex, and localized {{c1::ridge defects}} can complicate implant placement.

Stage IV periodontitis: considerable damage and significant tooth loss that impairs {{c1::masticatory function}}; needs comprehensive rehabilitation — without it the dentition is at risk of being lost.
Periodontitis may progress at {{c1::different rates}} in different individuals, respond less predictably to treatment, and may or may not influence systemic disease — which is what grading captures.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: periodontitis is a lifelong condition — "Once a perio patient, always a perio patient."

cloze.text: Grading indicates the {{c1::rate of periodontitis progression}}, responsiveness to standard therapy, and potential impact on {{c2::systemic health}}.
cloze.extra: It adds biological features: general health status and exposures such as smoking or metabolic control of diabetes.

cloze.text: Grade A = {{c1::slow}} rate of progression (low risk); Grade B = {{c2::moderate}} rate; Grade C = {{c3::rapid}} rate (high risk).
Whenever available, {{c1::direct evidence}} of progression (radiographic bone loss or CAL over 5 years) should be used for grading.
Grading by direct evidence (RBL or CAL over 5 years): Grade A {{c1::no loss}}, Grade B {{c2::<2 mm}}, Grade C {{c3::≥2 mm}}.
Grading by % bone loss ÷ age: Grade A {{c1::<0.25}}, Grade B {{c2::0.25 to 1.0}}, Grade C {{c3::>1.0}}.
cloze.extra: So if the % bone loss is higher than the patient's age, the patient is automatically Grade C.

cloze.text: Case phenotype: Grade A = heavy biofilm with {{c1::low levels of destruction}}; Grade B = destruction {{c2::commensurate with}} biofilm deposits; Grade C = destruction {{c3::exceeds expectations}} given the biofilm (rapid progression and/or early-onset patterns).
Grade modifier — smoking: non-smoker = Grade A; {{c1::<10 cigarettes/day}} = Grade B; {{c2::≥10 cigarettes/day}} = Grade C.
cloze.extra: So any smoker is at least Grade B. 1 pack = 20 cigarettes.

cloze.text: Grade modifier — diabetes: normoglycemic/no diagnosis = Grade A; HbA1c {{c1::<7.0%}} in a patient with diabetes = Grade B; HbA1c {{c2::≥7.0%}} = Grade C.
cloze.extra: So any patient with diabetes is at least Grade B. The book adds that an A1C of 5.7% or above means diabetic — that is not correct (ADA: 5.7–6.4% = prediabetes; ≥6.5% = diabetes); the AAP grade uses the diagnosis of diabetes and the 7.0% cut-off.

basic.back: No bleeding, no loss of attachment, probing depths 1–3 mm, and no modifying (or only well-controlled) risk factors — the ultimate picture of health

basic.front: What does "health on a reduced periodontium in a non-periodontitis patient" mean?
basic.back: There is clinical attachment loss from causes other than periodontitis (e.g., trauma, orthodontics, aging), but the periodontium is healthy now — no active inflammation, BOP <10%. It is not a history of periodontal disease.
An inflammatory response of the gingival tissues resulting from bacterial plaque accumulation at and below the gingival margin

basic.front: Gingivitis on a reduced periodontium: what is the crucial distinction?
basic.back: There is active (reversible) gingival inflammation on a periodontium that already has attachment loss, but the gingivitis is NOT causing new or progressive attachment loss — the loss is from a past event (e.g., treated periodontitis, recession) and is stable.

basic.front: Why can smoking delay the diagnosis of gingivitis or understate its severity?
basic.back: Nicotine causes vasoconstriction, so there are fewer classic signs of inflammation (less swelling and bleeding) despite underlying disease.
A white patch or plaque that cannot be scraped off and is not identifiable as any other disease; precancerous

basic.front: Vitamin C deficiency appears both as a modifying factor of plaque-induced gingivitis and as a cause of non-biofilm gingivitis. What's the difference?
basic.back: Modifying factor: mild deficiency worsens inflammation already driven by plaque (like a cold that hits harder when you're run down). Direct cause: severe deficiency (scurvy) itself produces gingival bleeding and soreness regardless of plaque. Always consider the primary cause of the inflammation.

typein.question: Periodontitis is "generalized" when at least what percentage of teeth are involved? (number + %)
typein.extra: Localized = less than 30% of teeth with CAL and radiographic bone loss. A third descriptor is the molar/incisor pattern.

typein.question: How many stages of periodontitis are there?
typein.extra: Stages I–IV, based on interdental CAL, amount and % of bone loss, probing depth, angular bony defects, furcation involvement, tooth mobility, and tooth loss due to periodontitis.

typein.question: Which periodontitis grade should clinicians initially assume before seeking evidence to shift it?
typein.extra: Then look for specific evidence to move to grade A or C.

mcq.question: A patient successfully treated for periodontitis 2 years ago returns. Probing depths are all 4 mm or less, BOP is 6%, and CAL and radiographic bone loss are present. What is the diagnosis?
options: A. Gingivitis on a reduced periodontium: stable periodontitis patient
B. Clinical gingival health on a reduced periodontium: stable periodontitis patient
C. Clinical health on an intact periodontium
mcq.answer: B. Clinical gingival health on a reduced periodontium: stable periodontitis patient
mcq.explanation: BOP below 10% with PD ≤4 mm in a treated periodontitis patient = health on a reduced periodontium (stable). Gingivitis would need BOP of 10% or more; an intact periodontium has no CAL or RBL.

mcq.question: A 30-year-old with recession from past orthodontic treatment (never had periodontitis) has BOP at 18% of sites and probing depths of 2–3 mm. Which diagnosis fits best?
options: A. Gingivitis on an intact periodontium
B. Clinical gingival health on a reduced periodontium: non-periodontitis patient
C. Gingivitis on a reduced periodontium: non-periodontitis patient
mcq.answer: C. Gingivitis on a reduced periodontium: non-periodontitis patient
mcq.explanation: BOP ≥10% = gingivitis; attachment loss from orthodontics (not periodontitis) = reduced periodontium in a non-perio patient. It is not periodontitis because the CAL is from a non-periodontitis cause.

mcq.question: A heavy smoker has thick plaque and deep calculus but very little gingival bleeding or swelling. What is the most likely explanation?
options: B. Nicotine-induced vasoconstriction masks the signs of inflammation
C. The patient has no gingival disease
mcq.answer: B. Nicotine-induced vasoconstriction masks the signs of inflammation
mcq.explanation: Nicotine constricts blood vessels, so smokers show fewer classic signs (less bleeding and swelling) despite disease — which can delay diagnosis. Increased vascularity is the mechanism for hormonal changes, which exaggerate inflammation.

mcq.question: Which of these gingival lesions has the HIGHEST malignant potential?
mcq.explanation: Erythroplakia (a flat red patch) carries a significantly higher malignant potential than leukoplakia, which is also precancerous. Frictional keratosis and smoker's melanosis are benign.

mcq.question: A 3-year-old has fever and painful, irregular, fibrin-coated ulcers on the gingiva that began as vesicles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Ruptured vesicles forming painful fibrin-coated ulcers in a young child = primary herpetic infection. Pemphigus vulgaris is a chronic autoimmune disease of adults; necrotizing gingivitis shows punched-out papillae and fetid odor.

mcq.question: A patient has interdental CAL of 4 mm at the worst site, radiographic bone loss of 25% (coronal third), no teeth lost to periodontitis, maximum probing depth 5 mm, and mostly horizontal bone loss. What is the stage?
mcq.explanation: CAL 3–4 mm, RBL 15–33%, no tooth loss and max PD ≤5 mm with horizontal loss = Stage II. Stage III would need CAL ≥5 mm, PD ≥6 mm, vertical loss ≥3 mm or Class II/III furcations.

mcq.question: Which finding by itself would shift a patient with Stage II severity to Stage III?
options: A. Maximum probing depth of 5 mm
mcq.explanation: Complexity factors can raise the stage: Class II or III furcation, PD ≥6 mm, or vertical bone loss ≥3 mm are Stage III. PD ≤5 mm, horizontal loss and 15–33% RBL all fit Stage II.

mcq.question: A 40-year-old non-diabetic patient smokes 5 cigarettes a day. Her worst site shows 60% bone loss. What grade is her periodontitis?
options: D. Cannot be graded without 5-year radiographs
mcq.explanation: Smoking <10/day starts her at Grade B, but % bone loss ÷ age = 60/40 = 1.5 (>1.0), which moves her to Grade C. Grading uses the whole chart, not just smoking or diabetes (Board Alert). Indirect evidence is used when direct evidence is not available.

mcq.question: A 50-year-old with well-controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.4%) has 20% bone loss and does not smoke. What grade applies?
mcq.explanation: Bone loss/age = 0.4 (Grade B range 0.25–1.0), and diabetes with HbA1c <7.0% is Grade B. HbA1c ≥7.0% or a ratio >1.0 would make it Grade C; there is no Grade D.
